title: The scribes
hook: companions wrote verses on palm leaves, bones and parchment, and many memorized it

segments.voice: Yesterday, juz': thirty parts, so the whole book can be read in a month. Your line was thirty parts, thirty nights. Day three hundred fifteen, the end of a week.

Medina, in the Prophet's lifetime. There's no paper mill in town. A new verse has just come to the Prophet ﷺ, and he calls for someone to write it down. What do you reach for? A palm stalk, stripped of its leaves. A thin, flat white stone. The broad shoulder blade of a camel, dried in the sun. A scrap of leather. And while the scribe writes, the people nearby are already saying it over to themselves, fixing it in memory.
screen: `NO PAPER MILL IN TOWN.` → `A PALM STALK, A STONE, A BONE.` → `SAYING IT OVER TO THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: The Prophet had a number of companions who wrote the revelation for him; later writers list many of their names. The one who stands out is Zayd ibn Thabit, a young man of Medina who often wrote at the Prophet's side. Years later, describing how he gathered the Qur'an, Zayd named what it had been written on: palm stalks, thin flat stones, and, as he put it, the chests of men. Other reports add shoulder bones and pieces of parchment. So there were always two copies: one scattered on whatever would take ink, one carried by heart. A story in Bukhari shows both at work. A verse came saying that believers who stay at home are not equal to those who strive in God's cause. The Prophet called for Zayd, with the board, the inkpot and the shoulder bone, and dictated it. Then a blind companion, Ibn Umm Maktum, spoke up: what about someone like me, who can't go? The verse came again with a few words added: except those who have a disability. Zayd wrote them in. The text answered the man in the room. And the memorizers? The Prophet named four people to learn the Qur'an from: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Salim, Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Others knew large parts by heart. That rounds out a week: the name, Qur'an, recitation; twenty-three years of it arriving; one hundred and fourteen surahs; each verse an ayah, a sign; Meccan and Medinan, split by the hijra; thirty parts. And now the people who held it, on bone and in the heart.
screen: `ZAYD AT THE PROPHET'S SIDE` · `PALM STALKS, STONES AND BONES` · `A VERSE ANSWERS A BLIND MAN` · `FOUR TO LEARN IT FROM`

segments.voice: Take a pen and any scrap, an envelope or a receipt, and write one verse you know, slowly, as if ink were rare: in Arabic if you can, in English if not, or just its first words. Then put the pen down, close your eyes, and say it once from memory. Two copies: one on the page, one in you.
The scribes. The companions who wrote the Qur'an down as it came, on palm stalks, stones and bone, while others kept it by heart. Today's word.
Your line: on bone and heart. Palm stalk, stone, bone, and memory. That's a week, done.

howItsDone: Muslims teach that the Qur'an was both written down by the Prophet's scribes as it was revealed and memorized by many companions, and they still learn it both ways: from the page and by heart.

fork.setup: a verse has just been dictated: those who stay home aren't equal to those who go. you're blind and can't go. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Ibn Umm Maktum spoke up, and the verse came again with words added for people like him: except those who have a disability.

original.note: Arabic: a scribe, one who writes. same root as kitab, a book.

trapdoor: what you thought: people who copied out a finished book.
what it means: companions who wrote each verse as it came, on whatever would take ink, while others memorized it.
what a scholar hears: Zayd's own list in Bukhari, palm stalks, thin white stones and the chests of men, and the four teachers named in Bukhari 3808.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4986 (Zayd: palm stalks, thin white stones, and the chests of men)
Qur'an 4:95 and Sahih al-Bukhari 4990 (Ibn Umm Maktum; 'except those who have a disability')

notes: Bukhari numbers 4986, 4990 and 3808 from memory; confirm.
Shoulder bones (aktaf) and parchment (riqa') come from other reports of the collection (e.g. in Ibn Abi Dawud, Kitab al-Masahif); confirm.
The paraphrase of the 4:95 exception (ghayru uli al-darar) as 'except those who have a disability'; confirm wording.
